item.title: Benchmarking Bolero
item.description:
Summary

Bolero predicts cell-state-specific ATAC signal and gene counts from DNA sequence. We benchmarked it in three settings. The main finding is that Bolero’s gains come from the ATAC background reference signal, Bolero’s most effective design choice, not from its AP-1 score.

  1. Seen cell state, unseen DNA. Bolero-10M’s test regions overlap the pretraining data of its Flashzoi trunk, so there is data leakage. We retrained Bolero on NeurIPS BMMC with Scooby’s split. Run from DNA alone, Bolero matches the published Scooby on both ATAC and RNA. It clearly wins only when the reference signal is supplied at inference.
  2. Unseen cell state, unseen DNA. In the preprint’s own DNA-only setting on the fear engram dataset, Bolero does not beat copying the control profile. With the reference signal, it ties or slightly beats copying.
  3. Unseen cell state, seen DNA. On the KA, Fear and MS datasets, AP-1 adds almost nothing. Measured, shuffled and random AP-1 scores give the same accuracy, and so does Bolero-10M, which has no AP-1 input. For ATAC, Bolero beats the copy-control baseline only when it receives the stimulated cells’ own embedding plus the reference signal, so the answer is already in the input. For RNA, it does not beat copy-control.
  4. Cell-state representation. In both the MultiVI embedding and the condition vector e, stimulation moves a cell type only about half as far as its average distance to other cell types. Changing AP-1 shifts every metacell by exactly the same vector regardless of cell type.

Overview of Bolero

  • About 75 similar cells inside each cell type × experimental condition are merged into one metacell. Metacells can share cells.
  • Neighbouring metacells are pooled into a pseudobulk of ~5 M ATAC fragments.
  • From 524 kb of DNA, the model predicts each pseudobulk’s ATAC signal (cut sites per 32 bp) and gene counts.
  • The gene head sits after the final conv, next to the ATAC head, and outputs a single count for that gene. A gene-body mask is a 0/1 track fed in alongside the DNA, which marks 1 from that gene’s transcription start to its end and 0 everywhere else. It is added to the output of the DNA conv stem.
  • Three encoders are concatenated into the condition vector e, the input of a hypernetwork that generates LoRA weights for every layer of the frozen Flashzoi backbone:
    • Cell encoder: the pseudobulk’s mean PMultiVI metacell embedding, plus the mean embedding of ~1,000 background metacells of the dataset.
    • Condition encoder: the released model uses only Tissue. The five datasets below have no condition encoder.
    • Shared encoder: species, and the pseudobulk’s AP-1 motif chromVAR score.
  • Reference signal is the dataset’s own bulk ATAC (the sum of 1,000 sampled metacells, scaled to 5 M fragments). It enters the model after the conv tower, before the U-Net/transformer.
    • Training: the reference signal is given, but dropped on a random 20% of batches.
    • Prediction: the reference signal is optional. With it, Bolero runs in signal-aware mode; without it, it is in DNA-only mode.

Bolero proposes using the AP-1 score to set the trans environment.

  • AP-1 is a TF family. Each AP-1 factor is a dimer, a JUN-family protein paired with a FOS-, JUN- or ATF-family protein. It binds the TGA(C/G)TCA motif.
  • Both FOS and JUN are immediate-early genes. When a neuron fires, Fos is transcribed within minutes. AP-1 then binds enhancers and recruits chromatin remodellers, turning on a larger set of late-response genes.
  • The AP-1 score in Bolero is computed from ATAC, as the AP-1 chromVAR score:
    • For each cell, chromVAR takes all peaks that contain the AP-1 motif and measures how much more accessible they are than expected from overall accessibility, resulting in a z-scored deviation.
    • The cells’ scores are aggregated and z-scaled on one common scale across all datasets, giving one number per pseudobulk.
    • A high score means the AP-1-bound sites in those cells are more open overall. The score is a second conditioning input, next to the cell-state embedding.
  • To predict the stimulated state: keep the control embedding and turn the AP-1 score up or down (for example, for the fear engram dataset the preprint dials the AP-1 score from −1.5 to +8, but the measured difference is only about +1).

Seen cell state, unseen DNA

Below is adapted from Bolero’s Figure 1c, d. Bolero did not compare with Scooby on RNA.

Bolero’s Scooby baseline is not the published Scooby. The Methods say only that “a hypernetwork head reproduces the published Scooby model”. In Bolero’s code, the “scooby” preset puts a Scooby-style head on Bolero’s framework, with plain rank-8 LoRA instead of Bolero’s cell-state-conditional LoRA.

We conducted an additional comparison experiment using the original Scooby and Bolero models. Both Scooby and Bolero were trained on the NeurIPS BMMC dataset, but they used different DNA folds. Thus, we retrained Bolero on the NeurIPS BMMC dataset.

The released Bolero-10M configuration validates on fold 0 and tests on fold 1, although the preprint says it uses Borzoi’s split. Its frozen trunk is Flashzoi replicate 0, which was trained on every fold except fold 3 (test) and fold 4 (validation). Bolero’s test and validation regions were therefore in the trunk’s training data, so there is data leakage (see table below).

To avoid this, we retrained Bolero on the same split as Scooby and its trunk: test fold 3, validation fold 4. Neither the trunks nor any retrained model saw the test regions.

Fold Scooby LoRA Bolero-10M LoRA Scooby trunk: Borzoi Bolero trunk: Flashzoi Bolero retrained
3 Unseen Trained Unseen Unseen Unseen
4 Validation Trained Validation Validation Validation
1 Trained Unseen Trained Trained Trained
0 Trained Validation Trained Trained Trained
2, 5, 6, 7 Trained Trained Trained Trained Trained

Neither Scooby nor Bolero reports a hyperparameter search. Scooby states that “due to computational constraints, extensive hyperparameter optimization was not performed”, and the Bolero preprint does not mention hyperparameter tuning.

Bolero has a published single-dataset training configuration (tutorial 06). We used that configuration to retrain Bolero on NeurIPS BMMC with fold 3 as the test fold. We directly used Scooby’s published model weights trained on this dataset. No hyperparameter sweep was done. We rebuilt the pseudobulks so that each contains one subclass only and no metacell is shared between pseudobulks (~5 M fragments each), matched to Scooby’s 21 cell types. Across-feature r is the mean of the 21 per-cell-type Pearson r. We then evaluated on fold 3.

Panel order in the figures below:

  1. Scooby (published).
  2. Bolero without reference signal: an ablation that never sees the reference, in training or at inference, so its input matches Scooby’s exactly.
  3. Bolero in its DNA-only mode: trained with the reference signal, run without it.
  4. Bolero in its signal-aware mode: the same model, run with the reference signal.
  5. Bolero-10M, shown for reference only, since it saw fold 3 during training.
  6. Dataset-average baseline. As every cell type gets the same value, it carries no cell-type-specific information.

ATAC

Cross-peak comparison:

Note that the published Bolero-10M model, which saw fold 3 of this dataset during training, has nearly the same performance as the retrained Bolero model, which did not see fold 3. Thus, the retrained Bolero model’s performance is not underestimated here.

Deviation r (subtract peak mean and cell type mean):

Bolero clearly outperforms Scooby only when the reference signal is added at inference. With or without the reference signal during training, Bolero has roughly the same performance as Scooby.

RNA

Because Bolero predicts gene counts rather than the RNA coverage that Scooby predicts, here we set the ground truth to be whole-gene 10x counts, matching Bolero’s training target.

To match Bolero’s whole-gene count, we also converted Scooby’s output to a whole-gene readout. For each gene, we sum Scooby’s predicted coverage on the gene’s strand across the entire gene body, exons and introns, using the same gene span as Bolero. Genes longer than Scooby’s 196 kb output window are covered with adjacent windows, and the results are summed.

Cross-gene r:

The dataset-average baseline scores highest here because across-gene r mostly reflects which genes are highly expressed overall, not cell-type differences.

Deviation r (subtract gene mean and cell type mean):

A similar conclusion is observed: without the reference signal at inference, the retrained Bolero’s DNA-only performance is approximately the same as Scooby’s. When the reference signal is added, Bolero outperforms Scooby.

Bolero-10M scores clearly higher than the retrained model. We cannot tell whether this reflects its leakage exposure to fold 3 or a weaker retrained gene model, so the retrained RNA results may be conservative.

Note that Bolero’s gene-count head rarely predicts values near zero, so unexpressed genes are systematically over-predicted.

Unseen cell state, unseen DNA

Figure 2g–j of Bolero examines the unseen cell types of unseen cell states. Bolero set up a baseline that reads out from the embedding of the nearest states, but did not set up a baseline that copies the observation of the nearest states.

The weights of the 18 individually trained models in Figure 2g–j have not been published, and the test split arrangement is not described either. Thus, we cannot conduct additional benchmarking experiments in the same setting.

In Figure 4, Bolero is evaluated on five datasets: fear engram (Fig. 4b), novel environment, stress, mouse visual experience and human visual experience.

Paradigm Cell type Prediction input pseudobulk Group 1 Group 2 Bolero’s AP-1 dial
Fear engram (Fig. 4b) Mouse hippocampus DG 24 h Trap− DG Fos-Trap+ DG cells, 24 h group 24 h Trap− DG (same group) +8 vs −1.5
Novel environment Mouse hippocampus CA1 Control CA1 Highest-AP-1-score CA1 cells, 1 h exposure sample Lowest-AP-1-score CA1 cells, same sample +5 vs −1.5
Stress Mouse hippocampus CA1 45 min handling CA1 Highest-AP-1-score CA1 cells, 15 min restraint sample Lowest-AP-1-score CA1 cells, same sample +1 vs −3
Mouse visual experience Mouse VIS L2/3 IT Earlier age group Age group (33.5, 35.5] Age group (25.5, 31.5] +5 vs −1.5
Human visual experience Human V1 L2/3 IT Prenatal Postnatal Prenatal +5 vs −1.5

For the novel environment and stress datasets, the evaluation is not independent of the model input, because cells are selected by AP-1 score and then predicted with that score.

The last two datasets (mouse VIS and human V1) have all their pseudobulks seen during training. For the other three, the published cell metadata (sample, experimental group, subclass) defines the input and comparison groups exactly for the fear engram (24 h Trap− vs Trap+ DG). For novel environment and stress, the input pseudobulk is defined, but the cells in the highest- and lowest-AP-1 groups are not published, and the preprint does not specify how they were split. Thus, we conducted the benchmark on the fear engram dataset.

We replicated Figure 4b from Bolero on the fear engram dataset.

Bolero Fig. 4a, b:

Our replication:

On AP-1

The authors publish a per-cell chromVAR score for each JASPAR motif, and we took the AP-1 motif (MA0478.2, the same motif the model uses). We averaged this score over all cells in a group and converted it to a z-score, as Bolero was trained on AP-1 values that are z-scores across pseudobulks. The authors’ own input file is not public, so this is what we measured: Fos-Trap+ = +0.70, Trap− = −0.31, which is much smaller than the preprint’s AP-1 score of +8 vs −1.5.

We used the input (24 h Trap− DG) to predict the perturbed group (24 h Fos-Trap+ DG) from the input’s embedding, dialed with the preprint’s AP-1 score and with our measured AP-1 score. We also directly predicted the perturbed group from its own cell embedding. All are compared against the baseline of copying the input pseudobulk.

No reference signal. This is the preprint’s own setting, as all Fig. 4 predictions were made in DNA-only mode. Here Bolero does not beat copying the control.

With the reference signal, Bolero ties or slightly beats copying.

On cell representation and the encoder

We then explored the cell representation and the encoder output e of all cell types between the fear engram groups.

Each dot is a metacell, and each panel highlights one cell type, with blue for its 24 h Trap− metacells and red for the “after” version over a grey background of all cell types. In the first two figures, red is that cell type’s Fos-Trap+ metacells, and in the third it is the same Trap− metacells with AP-1 raised to +8.

Cell embedding:

e of the embedding:

e with the AP-1 dial:

AP-1 only changes e. It moves every metacell by exactly the same vector. The moving direction is almost orthogonal to PC1 and PC2.

Below is the distance matrix between cell-type centroids. Rows of panels: MultiVI embedding, e, and e with the AP-1 dial. First column: distances between cell types within 24 h Trap−. Second column: Fos-Trap+ (rows) vs 24 h Trap− (columns); the boxed diagonal is how far each cell type moved. Third column: distances between cell types within Fos-Trap+.

The bar graph of normalized distances sums this up. Stimulation moves a cell type about half as far as its average distance to other cell types.

Unseen cell state, seen DNA

Bolero’s Hugging Face repository has five activity datasets. Their control groups were used in training, and their stimulated groups were held out.

Dataset Region Experiment Control group Stimulated groups
KA HPF Inject kainic acid to induce epileptic-like intense neural activity PBS (inject physiological buffer) KA2h (2 h after injection)
Fear HPF Fear conditioning *_Neg (unmarked cells) *_Trap (engram)
MultipleSclerosis Spinal cord MS mouse model Ctrl Early / Late / Peak of MS
EE HPF Enriched environment stimulation Ctrl EE1h / EE6h
Stress HIP Restraint stress Handling, 0 / 15 / 45 / 180 min Restraint, 0 / 15 / 45 / 180 min

Only Fear (Fig. 4b) and Stress (Fig. 4c) appear in the preprint. KA, MS and EE are not reported.

In the authors’ public records, pseudobulks are not independent. Neighbouring pseudobulks of the same cell type share metacells, and some mix metacells from control and stimulated samples. From now on, we drop the mixed pseudobulks and keep only pseudobulks that share no metacell with any other.

We left out EE and Stress. After this filtering, their stimulation effect does not replicate between two independent halves of the data.

The same pattern from before is also here: stimulation moves a cell type about half as far as its average distance to other cell types.

We ran ablations on them. Unlike Fig. 4, these use training-fold peaks, so the DNA was seen in training; only the cell state is new.

The preprint only gives AP-1 settings for specific groups, not for each cell type (see the table in the previous section), so we drew one random AP-1 value per pseudobulk from the preprint’s range [−3, 8].

We reconstructed the measured AP-1 score per pseudobulk with the same method mentioned above. In the “measured” settings, the model gets the stimulated pseudobulk’s own score. In the “shuffled” settings, the same scores are permuted among pseudobulks within each dataset.

We score only high-coverage peaks (genes), those with ≥ 10 reads (UMIs) on average. Below this, counting noise can dominate the profile.

The ceiling here is r between two random halves of each pseudobulk’s metacells, corrected to full depth (Spearman–Brown, square root; mean of 100 splits).

Light bars are without the reference signal and dark bars are with it.

The grey bar copies the matched control profile without any model, so it is the baseline to beat (dotted line). The red dashed line is the ceiling, i.e. how well the data agree with themselves. Moving left to right, the model gets more information about the stimulated state: first the control embedding, then the stimulated embedding. Each is run with Bolero-10M (no AP-1 input) and with the AP-1 model (Bolero-AP1-Score in the preprint) given measured, shuffled or random AP-1 in the preprint’s range. Coloured dots are the dataset means.

For ATAC:

AP-1 adds approximately nothing. Measured, shuffled and random AP-1 give the same r (0.80, 0.79, 0.78). Bolero-10M, which has no AP-1 input, also gives 0.80.

The reference signal helps in every setting. Only the stimulated embedding plus the reference signal beats copying the control (0.80 vs 0.77; ceiling 0.85). But the stimulated embedding comes from the measured stimulated cells, so the answer is already in the input.

For RNA, Bolero does not beat the copy-control baseline.

Gene expression changes little after stimulation, so the control profile is already very close. The reference signal helps. The stimulated embedding helps a little (+0.01 without the reference signal, +0.02 with it). Again AP-1 adds approximately nothing, as measured, shuffled and random AP-1 all give 0.85.

Acknowledgements

This benchmark was possible only because the authors released their code, model weights, data and tutorials, including unpublished datasets.

  2. Rauluseviciute, I. et al. JASPAR 2024: 20th anniversary of the open-access database of transcription factor binding profiles. Nucleic Acids Research, 52, D174–D182 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkad1059

item.title: Benchmarking seq2func models on distal enhancer effects with CRISPRi screens
item.description:
Summary

We benchmark six sequence-to-function genomic deep learning models — Enformer, Borzoi, Cerberus, NTv3, AlphaGenome, and AlphaGenome 2 — zero-shot on two K562 CRISPRi enhancer-knockdown screens (Fulco et al., 2019 and Gasperini et al., 2019), extending the in-silico CRISPRi setup from Karollus et al., 2023.

Four things stand out:

  • AlphaGenome 2 leads on the larger screen, Gasperini et al. (Pearson’s r = 0.53, against 0.45 for AlphaGenome, the next best). It is a clear but incremental improvement, holding out to about 100 kb from the TSS, with no gain beyond. On the smaller Fulco et al. screen, AlphaGenome 2 (0.75), Cerberus (0.70) and AlphaGenome (0.67) are statistically tied.
  • Cerberus, Borzoi’s successor, doesn’t improve on it overall. It is worse for enhancers near the promoter on the larger screen, and level or slightly better further out.
  • All six models systematically underpredict knockdown magnitude, and the gap to experimental measurements widens with enhancer-to-TSS distance. AlphaGenome 2 comes closest: on the larger screen its predictions are about 90% of the measured knockdowns on average out to 100 kb from the TSS, but under half beyond that — distal cis-regulatory element (CRE) effects remain difficult to predict.
  • AlphaGenome’s RNA-Seq head (with GENCODE-exon aggregation) beats its CAGE head on the larger screen — which output track you choose matters.

Code: seq2func_crispri_eval

Motivation

Sequence-to-function (seq2func) models keep getting bigger, longer-context, and more capable. AlphaGenome set the state of the art, succeeding Enformer (2021) and Borzoi (2024), and Google DeepMind has now released its successor, AlphaGenome 2 (November 2026), which conditions its predictions on a chosen cell type or state and is served through an API. Calico has also released Borzoi’s successor, Cerberus (2026), which replaces Borzoi’s attention layers and U-Net with bidirectional state-space (Mamba-2) blocks and reads 786 kb of sequence. DNA language models like NTv3 now compete in the same space by post-training on the same functional genomic tracks.

AlphaGenome was launched as a substantial step forward, with most of its zero-shot evaluation focused on single-nucleotide variant (SNV) effects. Two related weaknesses are especially well-documented for this class of model, both originally demonstrated on Enformer: predicting expression across personalised genomes (e.g. Sasse et al.), and predicting distal CRE effect magnitudes (how much knocking down a far-away enhancer changes its target gene’s expression). Both involve sequence perturbations the model wasn’t directly trained on, and both are where seq2func models historically struggle. Performance on these tasks is what tells us whether a model’s apparent advance translates to the questions biologists actually care about.

The personalised genome question is how well a model predicts gene expression for a specific individual from their own genome. It’s hard because the variants that distinguish one individual from the reference are sparse and small in effect, easy to lose against the much stronger reference signal a sequence model is trained to predict. Tu et al., 2026 and Kashyap et al., 2026 recently revisited it: AlphaGenome improves over Enformer on this task, but still falls well short of useful accuracy. The needle moves, but there’s a long way to go.

The distal-CRE magnitude question — much bigger perturbations, disabling a whole regulatory element — has received little attention since Karollus et al., 2023. They defined an in-silico CRISPRi benchmark on Fulco 2019 and Gasperini 2019 and ran it on Enformer and Basenji2, finding both substantially undershoot real enhancer effects. Borzoi, Cerberus, NTv3, AlphaGenome, and AlphaGenome 2 have all followed Enformer, claiming gains from longer contexts and broader predictive tasks — yet none have been evaluated on Karollus’s magnitude benchmark.

A related but easier task — enhancer-gene linking — has been tested more widely: in the original Enformer paper (Figure 1a), in AlphaGenome’s evaluation on the ENCODE-rE2G CRISPRi dataset (Figure 1b), and in the DNALONGBENCH benchmark. Linking is binary classification: does enhancer X regulate gene Y? A model succeeds by sorting interacting from non-interacting pairs above some threshold. Magnitude prediction is regression: how much does Y drop when X is disabled? It demands ranked and calibrated effect sizes across a continuous range, committing the model to a quantitative theory of enhancer-promoter regulation rather than a topological one. AlphaGenome leads on linking and notes that even it underestimates the impact of very distal enhancers — but doesn’t run the magnitude-prediction benchmark. Nor does AlphaGenome 2, which extends the lead on linking, most of all for distal enhancers.

We aim to address this. We re-run the Karollus benchmark on AlphaGenome 2, AlphaGenome, Borzoi, Cerberus, and NTv3 — and on Enformer, to anchor against Karollus’s original numbers. The result is a measure of progress on distal-CRE prediction across the last five years of seq2func releases, not just a test of AlphaGenome’s generalisation abilities.

Side note: CRISPRi (CRISPR interference) uses a catalytically dead Cas9 fused to a repressive domain to silence a target locus without cutting DNA. When the target is a distal enhancer, you can read out which genes go down in expression — giving you a measured enhancer → gene effect size.

Side note: “seq2func” = sequence-to-function. A model that takes raw DNA as input and predicts functional genomic signals (RNA-seq, CAGE, ATAC, ChIP, etc.) as output. Enformer, Borzoi, Cerberus, AlphaGenome, and AlphaGenome 2 were all trained end-to-end as seq2func models. NTv3 is a hybrid: first pretrained as a genomic language model (gLM) via masked language modeling — predicting hidden bases from their surrounding sequence across many species’ genomes — then post-trained on functional assays to produce seq2func outputs.

The benchmark

We test on two K562 CRISPRi enhancer screens:

  • Fulco et al., 2019 — ~60 validated enhancer–gene pairs from K562 CRISPRi-FlowFISH. Small but high-confidence.
  • Gasperini et al., 2019 — ~440 high-confidence significant pairs from pooled K562 CRISPRi at scale.

For each pair, the procedure is:

  1. Build a sequence window of the model’s native context (196 kb for Enformer, 524 kb for Borzoi, 786 kb for Cerberus, 1 Mb for NTv3, AlphaGenome, and AlphaGenome 2), centred on the gene’s TSS.
  2. Score the wild-type window.
  3. Dinucleotide-shuffle a 2 kb slice covering the enhancer. Repeat N = 50 times, average the model’s prediction.
  4. Aggregate the model’s K562 output. Enformer has no RNA-Seq output, so it is read from CAGE tracks in a TSS-centred 640 bp window (5 × 128 bp bins). The other five are read from RNA-Seq over the target gene’s GENCODE exons — AlphaGenome’s preferred RNA-Seq score, and how Calico scores genes with Borzoi and Cerberus. NTv3, AlphaGenome, and AlphaGenome 2 take the mean signal across the exons, averaged over K562 RNA-Seq tracks: all 86 for NTv3, and for the two AlphaGenomes the tracks that match the gene’s strand (3 of 5 for AlphaGenome, 8 of 12 for AlphaGenome 2). Borzoi and Cerberus sum the 32 bp output bins that overlap the exons, on the 71 of their 94 K562 RNA-Seq tracks that match the gene’s strand, after converting the output back to coverage with Calico’s inverse transform.
  5. Score pred_delta = (WT − mean(shuffle)) / WT per pair and correlate with the measured fractional knockdown.

Side note: This is a marginalisation procedure — by averaging predictions across many randomised backgrounds in which the enhancer’s motif content is destroyed, we isolate the enhancer’s contribution from the surrounding sequence context (the same idea underlies Global Importance Analysis (GIA); Koo et al., 2021). The background choice matters: N-replacement is out-of-distribution for the model and can produce strange predictions; drawing random bases changes local G+C content, biasing on composition rather than motif loss; even a plain base shuffle destroys dinucleotide frequencies like CpG counts, themselves a learned regulatory signal. Dinucleotide shuffling (Altschul–Erickson) destroys motif content while keeping both single-base and dinucleotide composition intact — the standard background for in-silico CRISPRi.

This protocol is a direct extension of Karollus 2023 — most of it is bit-for-bit faithful to theirs. We reuse their Fulco et al. evaluation tables (ziga_additional_columns.tsv + enhancer_knockdown_effects.tsv from their Zenodo release) with the same merge keys and validated-pair filtering, their TSS / enhancer / strand conventions, the same Enformer DeepMind checkpoint, and their K562 CAGE readout, central-bin aggregation, and Pearson/Spearman correlation framework. For Gasperini we apply the same protocol to the Cell 2019 high-confidence pairs (after hg19 → hg38 liftover). The model-specific adjustments — per-architecture aggregation conventions like 5×128 bp CAGE bins for Enformer, exon-overlapping 32 bp bins for Borzoi and Cerberus, exon-mean for NTv3 and both AlphaGenomes’ RNA-Seq — are architecture-driven; the evaluation harness around them is the Karollus harness. Four deliberate departures from Karollus are flagged in Limitations.

Each model is evaluated using its canonical published inference setup, with no test-time augmentations applied (TTA is explored separately for AlphaGenome below). Inference compute per pair therefore isn’t uniform: Borzoi runs four forward passes (one per fold) and Cerberus eight, while the other four run one — we compare models as their authors released them rather than artificially restrict Borzoi and Cerberus to a single fold. Enformer uses the lucidrains PyTorch port of the DeepMind weights — same weights as Karollus used, different framework wrapper. Borzoi predictions come from the Flashzoi community PyTorch port, evaluated as the original paper’s 4-fold ensemble (predictions averaged across the four published fold checkpoints). Cerberus uses Calico’s released PyTorch weights (baskerville), evaluated in fp32 as the 8-fold ensemble (predictions averaged across the eight fold checkpoints). AlphaGenome uses the PyTorch port loaded with the all-fold distilled checkpoint, a single model trained to reproduce the multi-fold ensemble’s behaviour. AlphaGenome 2 isn’t released as weights, so we query Google DeepMind’s hosted AlphaGenome API (Python client 2.0.0, all-folds model), conditioning every request on K562; the hosted model isn’t version-pinned, but two full runs on 12 November 2026 returned bit-identical predictions. NTv3 is InstaDeep’s revised 1 Mb-context checkpoint, NTv3_tracks_1mb, released alongside the v2 preprint (29 October 2026; HF revision a5a644f). As the model expects, its input is soft-masked (repeat bases in lowercase); shuffled enhancer bases keep the reference case at each position.

Results

AlphaGenome 2 leads on Gasperini et al.; on Fulco et al., AlphaGenome 2, Cerberus and AlphaGenome are tied. Figure 2 shows predicted vs. measured fractional knockdown for all six models on each screen, with points coloured by enhancer-to-TSS distance.

The matched-RF columns rule out the simple “they just see more sequence” explanation for the leaders: Fulco et al. barely moves (only one distal pair drops), and on Gasperini et al. the rankings are unchanged apart from NTv3 and Enformer, which swap fifth and sixth on Pearson’s r (0.29 vs. 0.30, then 0.31 vs. 0.30) — both AlphaGenomes even nudge up (AlphaGenome’s Pearson 0.45 → 0.46 and Spearman 0.45 → 0.48; AlphaGenome 2’s 0.53 → 0.58 and 0.52 → 0.57).

A few takeaways:

  • AlphaGenome 2 leads on Gasperini et al., the larger screen (Pearson’s r 0.53, against 0.45 for AlphaGenome and 0.37 for Borzoi). On the same 438 pairs it beats AlphaGenome significantly (Spearman’s ρ higher by 0.06, 95% CI 0.01–0.11; Pearson’s r higher by 0.09, CI 0.03–0.15; paired bootstrap), a gain about the size of AlphaGenome’s own lead over Borzoi. The gain holds out to about 100 kb from the TSS (ρ higher by 0.09, CI 0.01–0.19, n = 180, within 20 kb; by 0.08, CI 0.01–0.15, n = 175, at 20–100 kb) and disappears beyond it (0.00, CI −0.12 to +0.12, n = 83). AlphaGenome in turn leads the rest by a clear margin. On Fulco et al., AlphaGenome 2 (0.75), Cerberus (0.70), AlphaGenome (0.67) and Borzoi (0.64) are essentially tied — only AlphaGenome 2’s Pearson lead over Borzoi clears the noise, and only just (r higher by 0.11, CI 0.005–0.26; on Spearman’s ρ all four are level). See the small-sample caveat in Limitations.
  • Context length isn’t the explanation. NTv3 has a 1 Mb context, the same as both AlphaGenomes, but trails them on both screens (matched-RF Pearson’s r 0.51 vs. 0.67 and 0.75 on Fulco et al., 0.31 vs. 0.46 and 0.58 on Gasperini et al.). Enformer, despite its shorter 196 kb context (which excludes ~20% of Gasperini et al. pairs), is level with NTv3 on the pairs it can see (Pearson’s r 0.30) and not far behind Borzoi (0.37). Nor does Cerberus’s longer context (786 kb against 524 kb) lift it above Borzoi on Gasperini et al. (0.34 vs. 0.37).
  • Cerberus is weaker near the promoter, level or better further out. Against Borzoi, its predecessor, Cerberus ranks Gasperini et al.’s enhancers within 20 kb of the TSS worse (Spearman’s ρ lower by 0.14, 95% CI 0.04–0.25, n = 180; paired bootstrap) and is level beyond 20 kb (ρ higher by 0.05, CI −0.04 to +0.14, n = 237). On Fulco et al. it is level within 20 kb and ahead beyond it (ρ higher by 0.29, CI +0.02 to +0.56), though on only 26 pairs. Across all pairs the two are level on both screens.
  • On the same set of pairs, the AlphaGenomes still lead. Of Gasperini et al.’s pairs, 21 fall within the AlphaGenomes’ 1 Mb context but outside Borzoi’s 524 kb — so they contribute to the AlphaGenomes’ correlations but not Borzoi’s (Note, all of the tested Fulco et al. pairs are in Borzoi’s context). To make the comparison apples-to-apples, we restrict both to only the pairs Borzoi can also score: AlphaGenome’s Pearson’s r goes 0.45 → 0.44 and Spearman’s ρ stays at 0.45; AlphaGenome 2’s goes 0.53 → 0.54 and stays at 0.52 — giving essentially the same result.
  • The Gasperini et al. ceiling is low across the board. Even AlphaGenome 2 (Pearson’s r 0.53) leaves substantial variance unexplained. Some of this is likely measurement-side: Gasperini et al.’s scaled screen uses a high-MOI single-cell pooled design (median 28 gRNAs per cell), and the statistical and trans-perturbation challenges of high-MOI screens are well-documented (Barry et al., 2021). Fulco et al.’s CRISPRi-FlowFISH targets one enhancer at a time with a bulk-population readout, which we’d expect to give more precise per-pair effect sizes. We can’t separate measurement noise from model error from these correlations alone, so attributing the gap is interpretive — but it’s at least consistent with the per-screen difference we see. Either way, the headline framing is that AlphaGenome and AlphaGenome 2 improve CRISPRi prediction but a large gap remains, especially for distal cis-regulatory elements (CREs).

Side note: AlphaGenome 2 returns 12 K562 RNA-Seq tracks to AlphaGenome’s 5, so its score averages 8 strand-matched tracks rather than 3. That isn’t what lifts it: restricted to the three tracks matching AlphaGenome’s (polyA+ and total RNA-Seq on the gene’s strand, plus unstranded polyA+), it scores the same on Gasperini et al. (Spearman’s ρ 0.52), and seven of its eight tracks beat AlphaGenome on their own.

Predictions shrink, knockdowns don’t

Figure 3 plots observed and predicted effect against enhancer-to-TSS distance, to more closely match Karollus et al.’s plotting style.

Two patterns stand out:

  • Predictions are systematically smaller in magnitude than observed knockdowns. Even where the rank ordering is right (good Spearman), the predicted effect sizes are compressed, most of all for NTv3 and then Cerberus: the lines fitted to their predicted vs. measured effects (Figure 2) have slopes of 0.12–0.13 and 0.17–0.25, against 0.26 or more for the other four. AlphaGenome 2 is the least compressed by far, with slopes of 0.79 and 0.87, against 0.53 and 0.57 for AlphaGenome.
  • The gap grows with distance on Gasperini et al. There the measured knockdowns barely change with distance, but Enformer’s, Borzoi’s and AlphaGenome’s predictions fall towards zero, so their shortfall grows roughly 1.8- to 2.6-fold from the nearest pairs to the farthest. NTv3 falls short by a similar amount at every distance, because its predictions sit near zero throughout. Cerberus sits in between: it is already further short at the nearest pairs, and its shortfall grows about 1.3-fold. AlphaGenome 2 makes the pattern starkest: out to 100 kb its mean prediction is about 90% of the mean measured knockdown (about 60% for AlphaGenome), but beyond 100 kb it is under half (44%, against 28% for AlphaGenome). On Fulco et al., where the measured effects do decay with distance, the models capture some of that decay but less steeply than the data, most obviously NTv3 and then Cerberus; the two AlphaGenomes are the exception, decaying about as steeply as the data.

Is the distal shortfall just inaccessible enhancers? AlphaGenome 2’s preprint finds that much of the familiar drop in eQTL prediction with distance comes from variants outside accessible chromatin: inside accessible peaks, its sign and effect-size predictions hold up beyond 35 kb of the TSS. That can’t explain the shortfall here, because these screens target accessible elements: 98% of Gasperini et al.’s enhancers (94% of Fulco et al.’s) overlap a K562 DNase-seq peak from ENCODE. Splitting Gasperini et al.’s enhancers at the median DNase signal instead, distance still shrinks the predictions for the more accessible half: beyond 35 kb, AlphaGenome 2’s mean prediction is 0.82 of the mean measured knockdown, against 1.18 within 35 kb, while the measured knockdowns don’t change (0.32 vs. 0.31). Every model shows the same drop. Accessibility adds a second, separate bias: at every distance, Borzoi, Cerberus and both AlphaGenomes predict larger effects for the more accessible half, although the measured knockdowns of the two halves are about the same size (0.30–0.34). Beyond 35 kb, AlphaGenome 2 predicts under a tenth of the measured effect for 53% of the less accessible enhancers, against 22% of the more accessible ones. Splitting on H3K27ac (ENCODE) instead of DNase gives the same picture. So, to summarise, accessibility doesn’t explain the distal shortfall: nearly all of these enhancers are accessible, the models underpredict distal effects even for the more accessible half, and, separately, they underpredict the less accessible half at every distance. (Fulco et al. has too few distal pairs to split this way.)

A short aside: AlphaGenome’s RNA-Seq head, aggregated as the mean signal across the target gene’s GENCODE exons (their paper’s preferred approach), beats AlphaGenome’s CAGE head (we only compared heads for the original AlphaGenome) on Gasperini et al. (Pearson’s r 0.45 vs. 0.39). On Fulco et al. the difference is small (0.67 vs. 0.66). So if you’re benchmarking a new model on these screens, your output-aggregation choice should be considered carefully!

Linear vs. log₂ fold-change scoring

A second aside: we computed the predicted effect two ways. Figure 2 used the linear pred_delta = (WT − mean(shuffle)) / WT. We also computed log2(WT / mean(shuffle)) against −log2(1 − y_delta) — a log fold-change scaling that de-emphasises a few high-end outliers. Figure 5 shows the log2 version. Spearman is identical between the two scorings (rank-invariant); Pearson can shift noticeably, especially on Gasperini, and two pairs narrowly swap order: AlphaGenome and Borzoi on Fulco, and Borzoi and Cerberus on Gasperini — though the broad picture (AlphaGenome 2 first on both screens, and AlphaGenome, Borzoi and Cerberus ahead of NTv3) is robust.

Test-time augmentation: stabilising AlphaGenome

Karollus et al.’s original benchmark applies test-time augmentations (TTA) — for each sequence, run the model on 3 small offsets (−43, 0, +43 bp) crossed with both orientations (forward + reverse-complement), then average the 6 predictions. The 43 bp shift isn’t arbitrary: Enformer’s output is binned at 128 bp, and 128 / 3 ≈ 43, so the three offsets sample the TSS at roughly even thirds within its bin, averaging out where exactly the landmark falls. Genomic seq2func models have small but real positional sensitivity — predictions wobble across shifts — and TTA reliably damps this. Past work has shown the same effect in adjacent settings (Toneyan et al., 2022).

Side note: Test-time augmentation (TTA) means running the model on slightly perturbed versions of the same input and averaging the outputs, so the final prediction is less dependent on incidental properties like exact bin alignment or input orientation.

The headline benchmark (Figures 2–5) doesn’t use TTA, so all six models are compared on equal footing. To see what stabilising AlphaGenome’s predictions gains on this task, we ran a separate analysis applying Karollus et al.’s 6-pass recipe to AlphaGenome alone. Figure 6 shows the result: TTA improves AlphaGenome’s headline correlations on both screens, lifting Pearson’s r on Fulco from 0.67 to 0.69 and Spearman on Gasperini from 0.45 to 0.47.

Does ensembling help?

On the matched-RF (Receptive Field) set used in the headline table, a simple equal-weight average of the six models’ predictions doesn’t beat the best single model. On Fulco it falls just short of the best single models, AlphaGenome 2 on Pearson’s r (0.74 vs. 0.75) and Cerberus on Spearman’s ρ (0.57 vs. 0.58), well inside the small-sample noise (see Limitations). On Gasperini, where AlphaGenome 2 dominates, averaging in the weaker models clearly dilutes the predictive signal (Pearson’s r 0.51 vs. 0.58; Spearman’s ρ 0.54 vs. 0.57). Equal-weight ensembling, in other words, gains nothing over the best single model here.

Limitations

A few things to flag about our analysis.

Differences from Karollus 2023. We cross-checked our Enformer reimplementation against Karollus’s original code line-by-line with an LLM (Claude Opus 4.7). Our Enformer numbers don’t exactly match their published ones but the qualitative pattern is the same — Enformer underpredicts distal enhancer effects. Four deliberate departures from their approach may explain some of this gap:

  • Window construction. Karollus reads precomputed sequence_start/sequence_end from a fixed table, designed so both TSS and enhancer sit inside Enformer’s central crop. We build the window on-the-fly as strict TSS-centred so that all models were compared equally.
  • TTA only for AlphaGenome. Karollus et al. applies TTA (6 forward passes per sequence) uniformly across all evaluated models. Our headline six-model comparison (Figures 2–5) does not apply TTA to any model — each model is evaluated using its standard published setup: single forward pass for Enformer, NTv3, AlphaGenome (the distilled checkpoint), and AlphaGenome 2 (the all-folds model the API serves), the 4-fold ensemble for Borzoi, and the 8-fold ensemble for Cerberus. We separately apply Karollus et al.’s 6-pass TTA recipe to AlphaGenome (Figure 6) to characterise the stability gain, but we don’t apply it to Enformer, Borzoi, Cerberus, NTv3, or AlphaGenome 2.
  • No N-replacement control. Karollus also runs an all-N enhancer replacement (replacing every base with the “N” wildcard) as a stronger knockout than shuffling. We deliberately don’t: while reference genomes do contain N regions (gaps, centromeres, hard-masked repeats), these are typically excluded or under-weighted in training pipelines for these models, so a 2 kb block of N embedded in an otherwise-normal genic context is anomalous input. Predictions there reflect how the model handles unfamiliar input, not how it responds to motif loss, which is the actual question. The dinucleotide shuffle keeps the model in-distribution and isolates the motif-loss signal cleanly.
  • Linear vs. log2 observed effect. Karollus uses log2(1 + fraction_change); we report the linear fractional change and the log2 observed effect. Spearman is identical; Pearson’s r differs by a small log-vs-linear distortion.

These methodological differences may shift absolute Pearson values, though broad model rankings should be unaffected.

Small Fulco sample (n ≈ 63). Fulco et al.’s ~60 validated enhancer–gene pairs is small enough that correlation estimates carry wide confidence intervals — for r ≈ 0.65 at n = 63 the 95% CI spans roughly ±0.15 either side. Numerical differences within roughly ±0.05–0.10 (e.g., AlphaGenome 2 0.75, Cerberus 0.70, AlphaGenome 0.67 and Borzoi 0.64 on Fulco Pearson) should be read as essentially tied, not as a meaningful ordering. Gasperini’s ~440 pairs give tighter estimates, so the model gaps there are more reliable.

K562 only. Both screens are in K562, and K562 is heavily represented in every model’s training data. None of these numbers say anything about how the models would do on cell types under-represented in training. We’d expect the gap between models, and between predictions and truth, to widen there.

In-silico ≠ real CRISPRi. Dinucleotide shuffling destroys motif content but doesn’t capture chromatin context changes, dCas9 occupancy, or 3D genome reorganisation. It’s a motif-loss proxy, not a full simulation. Karollus discusses this; worth keeping in mind when reading the numbers.

CRISPRi isn’t purely cis. Knocking down an enhancer can affect other nearby genes, or the target gene’s own regulatory partners, whose altered expression shifts the cellular context against which we measure the target. Part of any measured enhancer effect is downstream of these indirect (trans) effects, which a sequence-only model predicting from a TSS-centred window can’t capture.

Implications

The benchmark tests seq2func models on experimentally validated distal enhancer-promoter interactions. AlphaGenome’s gains over Enformer on distal CRE effect-magnitude prediction are substantial, and most pronounced on the larger Gasperini et al. screen. That’s real progress. AlphaGenome 2 is a clear but incremental improvement on AlphaGenome: it ranks enhancers better on the larger screen and gets their effect sizes much closer to right, out to about 100 kb from the TSS. Beyond that, it ranks enhancers no better than AlphaGenome and predicts under half their measured effect. But the headline finding — that even AlphaGenome 2 underestimates the magnitude of distal-enhancer effects — converges with what AlphaGenome’s own paper observed on the easier enhancer-gene linking task on ENCODE-rE2G: distal CREs remain hard from two distinct evaluation angles. That AlphaGenome 2’s gain stops at about 100 kb contrasts with its own preprint, where its advantage on linking is largest beyond 100 kb. Linking a distal enhancer to its gene and predicting how much that gene drops are different problems, and the second is still open. Fully benchmarking seq2func models on distal CRE effect magnitudes will require follow-up CRISPRi screens in cell lines beyond K562 — without them, we can’t tell which gains generalise.

Echoing Tu et al., 2026 and Kashyap et al., 2026 from a different angle: AlphaGenome and AlphaGenome 2 improve CRISPRi effect prediction, but the remaining gap — especially for distal CREs — is still an open problem for the field.

The repo is set up so adding another model is one new scripts/test_<dataset>_<newmodel>.py writing a CSV with y_delta and pred_delta columns. If you’ve got a model you want to test, we’d love to see it!
